idiom_name: BCL empty instances (Array.Empty<T>(), Task.CompletedTask, NullLogger.Instance) + static readonly domain special case
implementation_notes: The .NET base class library already ships the common special cases - Array.Empty<T>(), Enumerable.Empty<T>(), Task.CompletedTask and NullLogger.Instance - so for framework interfaces the pattern collapses into returning the shipped instance instead of null. For a domain concept you write the same shape yourself: a sealed implementation with a static readonly Instance property, returned by the factory (this is literally how NullLogger is built). Nullable reference types and the null coalescing operator cover the one-line cases, but the language guidance is explicit that an invented sentinel is not a special case: only a value that satisfies the type's contract qualifies. Write the implementation when the degenerate case is part of the model; use a nullable return with `??` when the caller must make the decision.
pitfalls: A shared mutable instance is global state: keep the special case immutable and expose it as a static readonly field or a property, never as a settable singleton.
default(T) is not a special case: for a reference type it is null and for a struct it is the all-zero value, which may be a perfectly legal instance (id 0) rather than a designed case.
A NullLogger wired in as a fallback hides missing dependency-injection registrations, so logging silently disappears in production; make the choice explicit.
Overriding Equals/GetHashCode on a special case that shares one instance invites identity comparisons to succeed while structural comparisons still fail; decide which contract you mean.
